quote: I hate to say “So now let’s accept this and move on,” over such a philosophically controversial question, but it seems like a considerable majority of Overcoming Bias commenters do accept this.
content: The warrant offered for moving on is the agreement of the commenters on the author’s own blog. The book elsewhere warns at length against taking the consensus of a self-selected group as evidence (the essays on affective death spirals and evaporative cooling in Book II describe exactly the dynamic by which a blog’s commenters come to agree with its author), and the philosophical population that has actually studied the question divides the other way, as the survey figures in the annotation on Zombies! Zombies? show. None of this bears on whether the argument is sound. It bears on the essay’s self-presentation as a demonstration that “a considerable majority” has been convinced by, when the majority in question was convinced before the essay was written.

quote: And again, it’s not that “consciousness” is being equated to “that which makes you talk about consciousness.” It’s just that consciousness, among other things, makes you talk about consciousness. So anything that makes your consciousness go out like a light should make you stop talking about consciousness.
content: Clinical neurology has cases in which this fails in both directions. In Anton’s syndrome, patients with cortical blindness deny that they are blind, describe what they “see,” and confabulate explanations for their collisions with furniture (Maddula, Lutton and Keegan, “Anton’s Syndrome Due to Cerebrovascular Disease,” Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry, 2009); the talk about visual experience continues after the visual experience has, on every behavioural and physiological measure, gone. Anosognosia for hemiplegia is the same dissociation for the awareness of one’s own paralysis. In the other direction, patients with locked-in syndrome are conscious and cannot talk about it at all, and behaviourally unresponsive patients have been shown by functional imaging to follow commands covertly (Owen et al. (2006)). So the principle that a change which leaves one’s consciousness-talk intact has left one’s consciousness intact is false as a general rule about brains, and the “large step” the essay takes with the switch is one the clinic shows can go wrong. The essay is right that the switch is not going to do it. The reason is that gravity from a gram at ten metres does nothing to anything, not that the talk is a reliable gauge of the thing.

quote: Albert: “Suppose I replaced all the neurons in your head with tiny robotic artificial neurons that had the same connections, the same local input-output behavior, and analogous internal state and learning rules.”
content: This is Chalmers’s argument. “Absent Qualia, Fading Qualia, Dancing Qualia” (1995, in Metzinger, Conscious Experience; The Conscious Mind, ch. 7) runs the neuron-by-neuron replacement and argues, from the implausibility of experiences fading or flipping without the subject noticing, to the principle of organizational invariance: any system with the same fine-grained functional organization has the same experiences. That is Albert’s position, and the essay says its reasons for supporting Albert “shall have to wait for future essays.” They were published thirteen years earlier by the philosopher the previous three essays call deranged, as part of the same book that contains the zombie argument, and Chalmers regards the two as consistent: zombies are logically possible, functional duplicates are nomologically conscious. The identity question that Charles raises is Parfit’s (Reasons and Persons, 1984, the “physical spectrum”), and Parfit’s conclusion, that identity is not what matters, is where this book arrives in its later volumes. The dialogue is a good one. Its two live positions have authors, and one of them is the villain of the sequence.

quote: The makeup of future galactic civilizations may be determined by the answer…
content: The stakes are asserted rather than shown, but there is something to the point, and it is worth stating plainly because the sequence does not. Whether functional duplicates are conscious determines whether uploaded minds, artificial minds and gradually replaced minds are subjects of experience, and hence whether they are moral patients; the question is live in the ethics of artificial intelligence now (Schwitzgebel, The Weirdness of the World, 2024, for a survey of how unsettled it remains). The sequence’s method for settling it, the Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle, says that what preserves the causes of consciousness-talk preserves consciousness; the annotation above gives the clinical reasons to doubt the principle as a general rule, and the large language models that now produce fluent consciousness-talk with no plausible claim to the thing are the reason the “Zombie Master” the essay treats as a philosopher’s fantasy is a product one can buy. The principle would need, at minimum, a way to distinguish talk caused by consciousness from talk caused by training on a corpus of it. GAZP vs. GLUT tries to supply one by following the improbability back to the humans in the corpus. That locates consciousness somewhere; it does not say whether there is any in the machine, which is the question the galactic civilizations will need answered.
